theme: How long, O LORD?, the short lament and its resolution
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 13. It has only six verses. Read it three times, once for each of its three movements: the questions, the plea, and the song.
settingTheScene: This is one of the shortest laments in the Psalter and one of the most loved. David wrote it, but we do not know the occasion. Some think it came during the years he was hunted by Saul. Others think it was an illness. The lack of detail is deliberate. The psalm is meant to be prayed by anyone who has asked God, “How long?” It follows Psalm 10 and goes with Job: both are about holding on to God when God seems to be silent.
observation: The first two verses ask “How long?” four times: forgotten forever, hiding his face, taking counsel in my soul, my enemy exalted (vv. 1-2).
The psalmist says that God has forgotten him, and the sorrow is “in my heart all the day” (v. 2).
In verse 3 the psalm turns to commands: “Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes.”
He fears death: “lest I sleep the sleep of death” (v. 3).
He fears that his enemy will say “I have prevailed” (v. 4).
Verse 5 begins with a contrast: “But I have trusted in your steadfast love.”
The psalm ends in song: “I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me” (v. 6).
interpretation:
This psalm is built like a staircase. Each step is shorter than the last and leads upward. Verses 1 and 2 are four questions, and they are long and heavy. Verses 3 and 4 are three commands and a fear. Verses 5 and 6 are a statement of trust and a vow to sing. The rhythm of the poem acts out what happens in the heart of someone who prays honestly.

Pay attention to the phrase “How long?” It does not say “Why?” The question is not about the cause of the trouble. It is about duration. The psalmist can bear suffering for a season, but he cannot see an end to it, and that is what is crushing him. Many of us are in the same place. The pain is bearable only if it has a limit.

Then see what the psalmist asks for in verse 3. “Light up my eyes.” He does not ask for a change in circumstances. He asks for sight. His eyes are going dim with grief, and he wants God to revive them. That is a prayer for perspective, and it is a good prayer.

The turn at verse 5 is the heart of the psalm. “But I have trusted.” Nothing about the situation has changed between verse 4 and verse 5. The enemy is still there. God has not answered. What has changed is that the psalmist has chosen where to stand. He stands on God’s “steadfast love,” the covenant word, the word that means God will not walk away from his people. And from there he can do what seemed impossible in verse 1: rejoice and sing.

Notice that the song is a promise, not a report. “I will sing.” He is singing before the rescue comes, and the reason he can is that he has already received something: God has dealt bountifully with him, and he is looking back on it.
connection: Jesus prayed a lament of his own on the cross, quoting Psalm 22:1. Paul said that “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). Habakkuk 3:17-18 follows the same pattern: no fruit on the vines, yet “I will rejoice in the LORD.”
application:
When you are asking “How long?”, pray this psalm in the order it is written. State the pain honestly. Then ask God for light, not just for relief. Then say aloud, “But I have trusted in your steadfast love,” and name one specific way you have seen that love in the past.

If you know someone who is waiting, send them verses 5 and 6 and tell them you are praying that they will sing again.
prayerPrompts: Ask God “How long?” about the thing that weighs on you most.
Remember aloud some ways he has been good to you.
Tell him you trust him even here.
